title: CO2 Emission Hotspots and Dynamic Drivers in Jiangsu, China
content: City-level CO2 emission inventories and basic energy-consumption data are critical for carbon mitigation and low-carbon strategy formulation. However, recent studies remain deficient in systematic, fine-grained, and dynamic evolution investigations. This study aimed to identify CO2 emission hotspots and use the logarithmic mean Divisia index (LMDI) to measure the socioeconomic drivers of emissions across sectors in all prefecture-level cities of Jiangsu, China. The results indicate that the annual growth rate of Jiangsu’s CO2 emissions dropped from 7% between 2008 and 2013 to 2% between 2013 and 2023, mainly attributable to industrial structure, energy efficiency, and emission intensity. Combustion emissions increased 70.57%, from 566.0 to 965.4 million tonnes (Mt), during 2008–2023. Southern Jiangsu contributed 58.69% of 2023 combustion emissions, led by Nanjing (218.90 Mt). The energy industry and non-metallic minerals and metals averaged 35.14% and 32.48% of sectoral emissions during 2008–2023. Industrial structure, energy mix, and GDP per capita represented 46.10%, 42.11%, and 10.95% of summed positive full-period cumulative LMDI effects. The structural effect in Southern Jiangsu’s energy industry topped full-period hotspot rankings, whereas its energy mix effect led in 2017–2023 and 2020–2023. These shifts support differentiated mitigation assessment, subject to verification of energy and economic inputs.
